title: AI Leaders Are Refineries, Not Winners of Native Apps
dek: AI enters the agent era: first-phase leaders are just refineries, not winners of native apps; new platforms don't come from old platforms; organizations shift from roles to tasks; ultimately, humans compete on creativity that creates something from nothing.
why: Zeng Ming offers a three-phase industrial history framework to give you a coordinate system for locating AI's current position. It cures the optimism of "this time is different," and also provides realistic expectations for application entrepreneurs' opportunity windows and giants' transformation pains.
who: CEOs making AI strategy, executives at traditional giants seeking a second curve, AI investors, and tech founders torn between building models or applications.
skip: The rapid-fire Q&A and book list at the end can be skipped (after 2:29).

points.h: Building agents today is like building websites in 1992
points.body: Zeng Ming divides the industrialization of general-purpose technologies into three stages: first becoming social infrastructure, then an explosion of applications, and finally the emergence of native applications. In 2026, the consensus on token as a unit of measurement signals the maturity of the first stage; the agent events around the Spring Festival (commonly called "lobster") mark AI's official entry into the agent era. He compares it to the website-building movement of 1992: back then people built websites to share information; today they build agents to share capabilities. The browser hasn't appeared yet; whoever can establish agent standards and capture user entry points may be the biggest opportunity in the next two years.

points.h: A ten-trillion-dollar company will emerge, but not these two
points.body: Zeng Ming bluntly states that OpenAI and Anthropic are remarkable technical and commercial achievements, but business history shows that the first wave of companies to run out are likely not the big winners of the native application stage. Yahoo was worth $120 billion five years after founding, and AOL reached a valuation of $220 billion, yet neither became the Google of the next era. Model companies are more like AI cloud companies, refineries that extract base oil; the real application value belongs to chemical plants and car companies—and cars were not made by oil companies. He believes a ten-trillion-dollar company will definitely appear in the future, but it may not be the current leaders. Model companies will move toward a mature business of oligopoly plus strong government regulation.

points.h: The unit of AI-native organizations is tasks, not roles
points.body: Companies correspond to the hierarchical system of the industrial age. AI disrupts the industrial age, and the corporate system will decline. The basic unit of an AI-native organization is not a role but a task: people are not organized by reporting lines but flow according to "what problem needs solving," and both humans and AI collaborate around tasks. Therefore, well-designed positions and hierarchies will disappear, and traditional middle management will also die out. Future founders must first define the organizational task network. Silicon Valley's NewLab is a prototype of the new organizational form; OpenAI itself is more like a Lab than a traditional company. The culture of new organizations resembles a sports team, emphasizing transparency, sharing, and co-creation, not command and assessment.

points.h: Excellence is judged only in hindsight; being good is visible on the spot
points.body: Zeng Ming believes "excellent ≠ extraordinary." Excellence is growth sustained by positive feedback, while extraordinariness requires overcoming repeated negative feedback, persisting when everyone disapproves, and ultimately proving oneself a prophet of the era through enormous success. So "extraordinariness is determined after the fact." Those who are merely excellent easily fall into a cycle of self-validation, leading to conservative strategies. Extraordinary people have a small ego, tend to attribute success to the era and partners, and are mission-driven rather than externally valuation-driven. When identifying founders, he asks, "What kind of self would you be satisfied with ten years from now?" If the answer is "a ten-billion-dollar company," that is mainly self-driven, not an inner mission. Truly extraordinary founders are often altruistic and empathetic.

points.h: Strategy in the AI era cannot be planned; it must be generated
points.body: In the AI era, strategy is not planning but generation. Zeng Ming proposes a "strategy generation system": organizations must establish an environment and network that allows strategic insights to emerge naturally. Because decision frequency is higher and quality requirements are higher, CEOs cannot rely on linear extrapolation for planning, nor can they outsource strategy to McKinsey—McKinsey's rise was a product of the slow maturity of the industrial era. His methodology is "look ten years, think three years, act one year," with the core being "think three years": you must see at least two or three milestones ahead, creating tension between short-term actions and the medium-term picture. Organizational construction must ensure sufficient context rather than control, enabling the right people to make the right decisions at the right time.

points.h: The right analogy for robots is appliances, not cars
points.body: Zeng Ming believes robots are still in the strategic exploration phase, far from convergence. Currently there are two routes—building a generalized brain first or closing the loop in specific scenarios first—both logically valid, and it's impossible to judge in advance which is faster. Historically, the automobile industry had thousands of companies from 1900 to 1920, and it wasn't until Ford built the assembly line in 1913 that it entered scale; robots haven't yet had their Model T moment, and whoever truly sells ten thousand robots first is already remarkable. But a better analogy for robots is appliances rather than cars: after electricity was invented, refrigerators, washing machines, air conditioners, and countless other categories emerged. Robots interacting with the physical world will have N major scenarios, and home, companionship, and industrial uses may each produce their own native giants.

points.h: Giants that feel safe are the most unsafe
points.body: Zeng Ming says that in the face of a giant wave, no one is safe; feeling safe is the most unsafe. In business history, no company has ever smoothly transitioned from one era to the next. IBM and Microsoft are the only two possible exceptions, and both are full of uncertainty. AI is a productivity revolution that disrupts the industrial revolution, not a continuation innovation like mobile internet, so the technological reserves and organizational culture of old giants are liabilities. Google can survive as an AI cloud company, but it may not capture the consumer entry point; ByteDance has an AI cloud opportunity, but Doubao is not the future application; Tencent's social relationships will be restructured; Alibaba is not naturally safe either. New platforms are likely to be created by new companies.

points.h: Human value lies in creating from nothing, not in writing songs or painting
points.body: Borrowing Drucker's framework, Zeng Ming defines the AI era as the era of creativity: all knowledge work that can be structured will be taken over by AI. Humans are both forced and finally liberated to develop new potential. This potential is creativity—not writing songs or painting, but the ability to originally define complex problems and create something from nothing. AI has already taken all existing knowledge; human value lies in creating what does not yet exist. Therefore, he calls his mission "being a happy researcher" and believes the next step of civilization will reorganize around creativity. Even the education system will be forced to shift from "knowledge indoctrination" to "open exploration," because young people already know the old path leads nowhere.

An operating system that can directly dispatch all agents to complete tasks based on intent; Zeng Ming believes it belongs to the third stage and cannot be implemented yet.
A new organizational form dissatisfied with the corporate system, mainly composed of researchers; OpenAI is seen as the earliest example.
A Silicon Valley buzzword meaning taking control of one's own destiny, proactively seeking tasks and growth, replacing hierarchy-driven command.

quotes.text: The most successful companies must be counter-consensus, but counter-consensus does not necessarily succeed.
It may not survive to the end. It will likely do well later, but it is probably not the big player, the big winner in the native application stage.
Companies in the first stage find it hard to survive into the second stage, and companies in the second stage find it hard to survive into the third stage.

So companies will disappear; companies will die out. There's nothing to regret about that. In the future there will be more fun things. How many people go to work at a company happily now? They're not happy.

My technology is so strong, I've created so much value, why might my company not be worth much? Because of the basic law of economics: as long as there is homogeneous supply, you cannot capture high profits; you are just a company that isn't worth much.

Extraordinariness is determined after the fact, because you overcome negative feedback again and again, and when everyone disapproves of you, you finally prove with enormous success that you were the earliest prophet of the era.
I have always felt that in the face of a giant wave, no one is safe; whoever feels safe is the most unsafe.
